t.3.56.1: Seeing Lakṣmaṇa downcast in that lonely place, having come without Vaidehī, the righteous-souled son of Daśaratha questioned him.
t.3.56.2: She who followed me when I set out for the Daṇḍaka forest, where is that Vaidehī, O Lakṣmaṇa, whom you have abandoned to come here?
t.3.56.3: Where is Vaidehī, slender-waisted, my companion in sorrow, to me who am fallen from the kingdom, wretched, wandering about the Daṇḍaka forests?
t.3.56.4: O hero, where is that Sītā, the companion of my life, who resembles a daughter of the gods, without whom I cannot bear to live even for a moment?
t.3.56.5: O Lakṣmaṇa, I would not desire lordship over the immortals or even over the earth without her, the daughter of Janaka, radiant like burnished gold.
t.3.56.6: Is Vaidehī, dearer to me than my very life, still alive? Gentle one, I hope my exile will not prove to have been in vain?
t.3.56.7: O Saumitri, when I have died on account of Sītā and you have gone back, will that Kaikeyī then be happy, with her desire fulfilled?
t.3.56.8: Gentle one, will not the wretched Kausalyā, her son now dead, have to wait in attendance upon Kaikayī, who has attained her aim and holds the kingdom together with her son?
t.3.56.10: If Vaidehī, Sītā, does not again speak to me with a smile when I have reached the hermitage, I shall perish, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.56.9: If Vaidehī is alive, I shall go back to the hermitage; but if that virtuous lady has passed away, I shall give up my life, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.56.11: Tell me, Lakṣmaṇa, whether Vaidehī is alive or not, or whether, while you were negligent, the poor ascetic lady has been devoured by the rākṣasas.
t.3.56.12: Tender and young, and one who has never known sorrow, Vaidehī, downcast in mind, is surely grieving over her separation from me.
t.3.56.14: I suspect that Vaidehī heard that cry, which resembled my voice, and that you, sent by her in her terror, came here quickly to see me.
t.3.56.13: Surely fear was aroused even in you by that crooked, utterly wicked rākṣasa as he cried aloud, “Lakṣmaṇa!”
t.3.56.15: In every way a grievous wrong has been done by you in abandoning Sītā in the forest; an opportunity has been given to the cruel rākṣasas to strike back.
t.3.56.16: The flesh-eating rākṣasas are grieved by the slaying of Khara; by those dreadful ones Sītā will surely have been killed, there is no doubt.
t.3.56.18: Thus thinking of Sītā of the beautiful hips, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, came in haste to Janasthāna.
t.3.56.17: Alas, O destroyer of foes, I am utterly sunk in calamity! But what shall I do now? I suspect that such a fate was bound to befall me.
t.3.56.19: Reproaching his younger brother, who looked stricken, and sighing deeply from hunger, weariness and thirst, his mouth parched and his heart dejected, he reached his dwelling and saw that it was empty.
t.3.56.20: Entering his own hermitage and following some of the places where they used to stroll for pleasure, the hero thought, "This is that very place," and there in their dwelling-ground, his hair standing on end, he became deeply distressed.
